newsitem.title: FRANCE: Costly French reactor, "penguins' airstrip" rapped.
newsitem.headline: Costly French reactor, "penguins' airstrip" rapped.

text.p: France's public spending watchdog has denounced a 60 billion franc ($12 billion) bill for the Superphenix fast-breeder nuclear reactor and an Antarctic airstrip which only flightless penguins seem to use, a newspaper reported on Saturday.

The annual report by the magistrates of the Court of Accounts, leaked to the daily Liberation, pinpoints a litany of waste or mispending, including an unpaid two billion franc ($400 million) telephone bill the state owes France Telecom.

The report, to be officially unveiled on Monday, says the state has spent 60 billion francs on Superphenix at Creys-Malville near the Swiss border, a fault-plagued reactor which has operated for only a dozen months since it was commissioned 20 years ago. A year ago it was turned into a research laboratory.
"There are still question marks over the usefulness and durability of this installation," the magistrates noted, according to Liberation.
No official comment on the report was available.

The report was quoted as saying the 110 million franc ($22 million) airstrip in French-owned Terre Adelie in western Antarctica, completed in 1993 after a seven-year construction, had never been used.

From February to September, aircraft cannot land there because of poor weather conditions. From October to January, the strip is unusable because of a decree by the Environment Ministry protecting the site as a breeding ground used by penguins and petrels among other birdlife.

The report, according to the paper, also denounced state-owned SNCF railways for spending more than two billion francs ($400 million) on Socrate, a computerised ticket booking system based on new charges. The Court said the railways had bet on a 50 percent jump in traffic on main lines in 1986-1995 but that in fact traffic had fallen by five percent in that period.

The Court also highlighted what it said were extravagant spending on computer equipment and fraudulous expense claims at the National Book Centre. Over three years, it was quoted as saying, six publishers each managed to accumulate more than 3.5 million francs ($700,000) in state subsidies from the body.

"Every year, at about the same time as the grape harvest, the Court of Accounts throws a tragi-comic stone into the national pond which is a quickly forgotten joke," Liberation said in an accompanying editorial.

"...There is one scandal however which the Court does not question: the reasons for its own uselessness, as virtually all its labours in the past half-century have been buried without trace, or almost," it added.
